content: 1. The process of diagnosing tuberculosis (TB) begins with an individual experiencing symptoms of active TB that they recognize as serious. 2. The individual must have access to healthcare and seek medical attention at an appropriate health facility. 3. A healthcare worker must accurately assess whether the individual meets the criteria for suspected TB. 4. A diagnostic algorithm with adequate sensitivity and specificity must be successfully applied to confirm the diagnosis. Passive case-finding for TB may include systematic screening if all individuals seeking care at a health facility are systematically evaluated for TB symptoms. Rescreening involves repeated screening of the same population at specific intervals. A risk group for TB is defined as any group of individuals with a significantly higher prevalence or incidence of TB compared to the general population. This may include individuals with specific risk factors, such as close contact with someone with active TB, living with HIV, having diabetes, or residing in high-burden areas like urban slums or prisons. Screening tests for active TB are designed to distinguish individuals with a high likelihood of having active TB from those who are unlikely to have the disease. These tests are not diagnostic but serve to identify individuals who require further diagnostic evaluation. Second screening tests are applied to individuals who tested positive during the initial screening to confirm or rule out active TB. Systematic screening for active TB involves the organized identification of individuals with suspected TB in a predetermined target group using rapid tests, examinations, or procedures. Those who screen positive must undergo diagnostic tests and clinical assessments to confirm the diagnosis with high accuracy. Systematic screening can target the entire population (mass screening) or specific risk groups. It can also focus on individuals seeking healthcare or those who do not seek care due to barriers or lack of perceived health problems. Passive case-finding and systematic screening are complementary approaches. Screening is typically provider-initiated and offered to a defined target group. Risk groups for TB include individuals with higher TB prevalence or incidence due to shared risk factors or living conditions. These groups may include people living with HIV, individuals with diabetes, prisoners, healthcare workers, and residents of high-burden areas. The absolute level of TB prevalence or incidence can be used as a threshold to define risk groups, which may vary by region and change over time. Screening for TB in high-risk groups can help reduce delays in diagnosis and improve early detection. However, other interventions to enhance healthcare access and health-seeking behavior may also be effective and cost-efficient, depending on the local context. Early detection of TB is particularly important for vulnerable groups, such as people living with HIV, young children, the elderly, and individuals with compromised immune systems. Delayed diagnosis in these groups increases the risk of poor treatment outcomes, including relapse and death. The primary objective of TB screening is to detect active TB early, which helps reduce poor treatment outcomes, health sequelae, and adverse social and economic consequences for individuals. Early detection also shortens the duration of infectiousness, reducing TB transmission and incidence. Screening can also identify individuals eligible for latent TB infection treatment, such as people living with HIV or young children in contact with TB cases. Additionally, it can identify individuals at high risk of developing active TB in the future, who may require repeat screening. Combining TB screening with screening for TB risk factors can help map individual or community-level risk factors and socioeconomic determinants, enabling more effective disease prevention strategies. The global incidence of TB is declining slowly, at less than 2% per year. To achieve the TB elimination target of fewer than 1 case per 100,000 population by 2050, the incidence must decline by 20% per year. Missed or delayed TB diagnoses and limited access to high-quality care increase the risk of death, suffering, long-term complications, and catastrophic financial consequences, particularly for the poorest populations. Passive case-finding relies on individuals recognizing symptoms, seeking care, being correctly assessed by healthcare workers, and undergoing a complete diagnostic algorithm. Barriers at any step disproportionately affect the poorest individuals, who face the greatest challenges in accessing high-quality services and bear the highest costs of illness and healthcare. Systematic screening can be particularly beneficial for vulnerable groups, but ensuring optimal diagnostic procedures for those actively seeking care is the first essential step. The ultimate goals of TB screening are to reduce the prevalence and mortality of TB and to decrease TB transmission by shortening the duration of infectiousness. Screening guidelines must be adapted to local settings, and national and subnational recommendations should guide healthcare staff in specific contexts. Operational guidance for planning and implementing TB screening in specific risk groups will be provided in future publications.
